title: Starting a Child Care Center in Montana: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

Introduction

Starting a Child Care Facility in Montana represents a meaningful opportunity to serve children and working families while building a compliant, sustainable care business. The state is currently experiencing a critical shortage of quality child care, creating a clear path for entrepreneurs dedicated to early childhood education and development. Oversight and funding are administered by the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) through its Child Care Licensing (CCL) program, with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through the same department for state and federal subsidy programs.

With significant child care deserts affecting 59% of counties and licensed capacity meeting only 43-44% of the estimated statewide demand, Montana offers a high-need market for providers. While reimbursement rates of approximately $58 per full day for infant care and state grants are available, success depends on a provider’s ability to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements effectively. The need is particularly acute for infant and toddler care, where capacity meets only 31% of demand.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Child Care Program in Montana, from understanding DPHHS regulations and licensing to staffing, securing funding, and preparing for inspections. Whether you are planning a small family home or a large child care center, this comprehensive overview will provide the foundation you need to succeed.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Montana’s Child Care Facility Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Montana’s Child Care Facility Regulations

Before you can serve a single child, you must have a deep understanding of the state’s regulatory landscape. Montana regulates Child Care Facilities through the Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) Child Care Licensing (CCL) program. This agency is responsible for overseeing the licensing, regulation, and ongoing compliance for all registered and licensed child care programs in the state.

Providers who plan to accept state subsidies by serving families in the Best Beginnings Child Care Scholarship program must also comply with rules set by DPHHS, which administers federal funds from the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF). This federal framework adds layers of requirements related to quality standards, health and safety training, and reporting.

The regulatory framework, outlined in the Administrative Rules of Montana (ARM) Title 37, Chapter 101, emphasizes child safety, staff qualifications, and program quality. Key areas of focus include maintaining proper staff-to-child ratios, ensuring a safe physical environment, conducting comprehensive background checks, and documenting all aspects of your operation. Licenses typically require annual or biennial renewal, contingent on successful inspections and adherence to all state rules.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Your next step is to decide on the specific service model that best fits your vision and resources. Montana supports multiple Child Care Program variants, each with different licensing, staffing, and facility requirements. Understanding these distinctions is crucial for your business plan and license application.

Montana’s primary child care license types include:

  • Family Child Care Home: A program operated in the provider’s own residence, licensed to care for 3 to 6 children. This model offers a lower-cost entry point and a home-like environment.
  • Group Child Care Home: A program that can be operated in a residence or a commercial space, licensed to care for 7 to 15 children. This model requires more staff and space than a family home but serves more children.
  • Child Care Center: A program typically operated in a commercial facility, licensed to care for 16 or more children. This is the largest model, requiring a dedicated director, multiple classrooms, and adherence to the most stringent facility and staffing regulations.

Program size typically ranges from 3 children in a small family home to over 100 in a large center. While demand is strong statewide, it is most critical in rural counties and areas with high workforce participation, which are often designated as child care deserts. The demand for infant and toddler slots is a significant unmet need across all regions. While urban centers have more competition, areas with lower penetration represent a massive opportunity for new providers to become essential community resources.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

With a program type selected, you can formalize your business and begin the official licensing process. Most providers in Montana operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or S-Corporation to protect their personal assets. Regardless of your choice, you must complete several foundational steps:

  • Register your business name and structure with the Montana Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, which is necessary for hiring employees and opening a business bank account.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability and, if you have employees, workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a complete licensing application to the DPHHS Child Care Licensing (CCL) program. This application is extensive and requires detailed information about your business, facility, program director, and policies.

Be prepared for a thorough process. Licensing timelines in Montana generally range from 4 to 9 months, depending on the completeness of your application, the time it takes to prepare your facility, and the scheduling of your initial inspection. Incomplete paperwork or a facility that doesn’t meet code are the most common causes of delay.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your roadmap to a sustainable operation. It forces you to analyze your finances and prove that your child care program can be both a community asset and a viable business. Startup costs in Montana typically range from $10,000 – $50,000 for a Family Home to $75,000 – $250,000+ for a new Child Care Center, depending on real estate and renovation needs.

Operating expenses are a critical component of your plan. In child care, these are driven primarily by staffing, which often represents 50-60% of total costs. Other major expenses include rent/mortgage, utilities, insurance, food, and educational supplies.

Your revenue will come from a mix of private-pay tuition and public subsidies. A snapshot of typical revenue sources includes:

  • State Subsidy Reimbursement: Through the Best Beginnings program, rates are approximately $58 per full day and $29 per half-day for infant/toddler care (as of March 2024).
  • Private Pay Tuition: Rates are set by the provider and are typically higher than subsidy rates. Market research is essential to set competitive yet profitable rates for your area.
  • Grant Funding: Montana offers grant programs, such as a $2 million pool for workforce development and infrastructure (2024-2025), which can provide crucial capital.

Due to high operating costs, the report notes an “extended break-even timeline.” Providers operating at a target occupancy of 85-90% can generally achieve 5% to 15% profit margins, but this requires meticulous financial management.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Your physical location must be safe, welcoming, and compliant with all DPHHS regulations. Whether you are using your home or a commercial building, the facility is one of the most scrutinized aspects of your license application. Key facility requirements include:

  • Minimum indoor and outdoor square footage per child.
  • Safe, fenced outdoor play areas with appropriate ground cover and no hazards.
  • Adequate, child-accessible bathroom facilities.
  • A food preparation area that meets local health department codes.
  • Full compliance with state and local fire, safety, and building codes, including functional smoke detectors, fire extinguishers, and clear emergency exits.
  • Proper lighting, ventilation, and heating.

When selecting a location, consider more than just the building itself. Analyze local zoning laws to ensure a child care business is permitted. Evaluate the site’s accessibility for parents, proximity to elementary schools and large employers, and the availability of a qualified workforce in the area.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your staff is the heart of your program. Montana’s regulations set clear minimums for staffing ratios and qualifications to ensure the safety and well-being of children. Required roles in a center typically include:

  • Facility Director/Administrator: Must meet specific educational and experience requirements to oversee all operations, compliance, and staff management.
  • Lead Teachers: Responsible for classroom management, curriculum implementation, and communication with parents.
  • Assistant Teachers/Aides: Support lead teachers and help maintain required staff-to-child ratios.

Montana’s staff-to-child ratios are strict and must be maintained at all times:

  • Infants: 1 staff member for every 4 infants (1:4)
  • Toddlers: 1 staff member for every 6 toddlers (1:6)
  • Preschoolers: 1 staff member for every 10 preschoolers (1:10)
  • School-age Children: 1 staff member for every 20 children (1:20)

All staff must undergo comprehensive background checks and complete required training, including First Aid and CPR certification, initial orientation on health and safety, and annual continuing education hours in topics related to child development and safety. Given Montana’s workforce shortages, creating a competitive compensation package and a positive work environment is key to attracting and retaining qualified, passionate educators.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Written policies and procedures are the operational backbone of your child care program. They ensure consistency, promote safety, and are a mandatory component of your licensing application. DPHHS requires comprehensive written policies covering all aspects of your operation, including:

  • Health and Safety Procedures: Handwashing, diapering, sanitation, and illness exclusion.
  • Emergency and Disaster Plans: Detailed procedures for fire, severe weather, medical emergencies, and facility lockdowns.
  • Behavior Management and Positive Discipline: Your approach to guiding children’s behavior without the use of prohibited punishments.
  • Medication Administration: Secure storage and documentation for administering medication to children.
  • Enrollment, Attendance, and Fee Collection: Clear policies for parents regarding schedules, payments, and absences.
  • Staff Hiring, Training, and Supervision: Your process for vetting, onboarding, and managing employees.
  • Safe Sleep Practices for infants to prevent SIDS.

In addition to facility-wide policies, you must develop, review, and document individual care plans for each child, especially for infants and those with special needs. These plans, created in partnership with parents, outline feeding schedules, allergy information, and any specific needs, ensuring personalized and safe care.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

In a market with as much unmet demand as Montana, your best marketing strategy is operational excellence. While traditional advertising can play a role, successful providers focus on building a reputation for compliance, responsiveness, and high-quality care. Referrals will be your primary driver of enrollment.

Key referral sources for child care in Montana typically come from:

  • State Child Care Resource and Referral (CCR&R) Agencies: Getting listed with these agencies is critical, as they are the first point of contact for many parents, especially those seeking subsidies.
  • Local Employers and HR Departments: Partnering with large local businesses to offer child care solutions for their employees can create a stable enrollment pipeline.
  • Online Directories and Parent Groups: Maintaining a professional website and a positive presence on local social media parenting groups builds trust and visibility.
  • Word-of-Mouth from Current Families: Happy parents are your most powerful advocates. Excellent communication and care will lead to powerful organic growth.
  • Partnerships with Local Schools and Community Organizations: Building relationships with elementary schools, pediatricians, and family service organizations can generate consistent referrals.

Focus on showcasing your program’s strengths: your qualified staff, your clean and safe facility, and your commitment to regulatory compliance. This builds the trust necessary to attract and retain families.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Receiving your license is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Ongoing oversight is conducted by the DPHHS Child Care Licensing (CCL) program, whose surveyors will conduct both scheduled and unannounced inspections of your facility.

These inspections are comprehensive, with surveyors focused on identifying common deficiencies, which often include:

  • Incorrect staff-to-child ratios, even for brief periods.
  • Incomplete staff files, such as missing background checks or outdated training certificates.
  • Environmental safety hazards, like uncovered electrical outlets, accessible cleaning supplies, or unsafe playground equipment.
  • Improper documentation of attendance, incident reports, or medication administration.

To ensure you are always ready for an inspection, foster a culture of continuous quality improvement. Conduct your own regular self-audits, keep meticulous records, and ensure all staff are consistently trained on your policies. Audit-ready documentation and a proactive approach to safety are essential for maintaining your license in good standing and building a reputable program.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does it take to open a child care program in Montana?

A: Typically 4 to 9 months. The timeline depends heavily on the license type (Family, Group, or Center), your readiness, the completeness of your application, and the DPHHS review and inspection process. Delays are often caused by incomplete paperwork or facility issues.

Q: What licenses are required to open a child care program in Montana?

A: You need a license from the DPHHS Child Care Licensing program. The specific type of license—Family Child Care Home, Group Child Care Home, or Child Care Center—depends on the number of children you plan to serve.

Q: What reimbursement is available for child care in Montana?

A: Montana offers state subsidies through the Best Beginnings Child Care Scholarship program. As of early 2024, reimbursement rates are around $58 per day for infants. Providers can also accept private pay tuition and may be eligible to apply for state grants for workforce development and facility infrastructure.

Conclusion

Starting a Child Care Facility in Montana is a challenging but immensely rewarding venture. The state’s significant need for quality care, particularly for infants and toddlers and in rural counties, presents a clear and compelling opportunity. Success requires careful planning, a deep understanding of DPHHS regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. Providers who invest in compliance, build a dedicated and qualified staff, and cultivate strong community and referral relationships are positioned for long-term success and a lasting positive impact on Montana’s families.
